alignment.note: The Greek genitive absolute (καταβαινόντων) and the Latin ablative absolute (descendentibus) both encode the temporal circumstantial clause through case morphology, whereas the Syriac employs a finite clause introduced by the conjunction ܘܟܕ ('and when') with the participle ܢܚܬܝܢ, a typical Semitic temporal construction.

The Greek transitional particle δέ ('now, but') is left untranslated in both the Peshitta and the Vulgate, which is routine since neither Syriac nor Latin requires a discourse particle here and the connective force is already carried by the initial conjunction.

Greek expresses the subject of the absolute construction explicitly with αὐτῶν, matched by Latin illis; the Peshitta encodes the third-person plural subject inflectionally within the participle ܢܚܬܝܢ and supplies no separate pronoun, a normal Syriac economy.

Greek and Latin both render the articular/definite phrase ('from the mountain', ἐκ τοῦ ὄρους / de monte), while the Syriac ܡܢ ܛܘܪܐ omits any explicit article, definiteness being unmarked here; the Vulgate also attaches a comma after monte.

Greek and Latin use a simple aorist/perfect finite verb (διεστείλατο / præcepit), whereas the Syriac forms a periphrastic past with the participle ܡܦܩܕ plus the auxiliary ܗܘܐ ('was commanding'), the standard Syriac means of expressing past durative or background action.

Greek introduces the content of the command with the conjunction ἵνα governing a subjunctive; both Latin (ne ... narrarent) and Syriac (ܕ- ... ܠܐ ܢܐܡܪܘܢ) absorb this into a negated final/jussive clause without a separate positive conjunction.

Greek compresses the prohibition into the single negative indefinite μηδενί ('to no one'); Latin analyses it into ne ... cuiquam and Syriac into ܕܠܐܢܫ ... ܠܐ ('to anyone ... not'), distributing the negation across two words as their grammars require.

Greek uses the somewhat fuller verb διηγέομαι ('to recount in detail'), whereas the Peshitta ܢܐܡܪܘܢ and the Vulgate narrarent employ the more general verbs 'to say/tell'; the Vulgate additionally inserts a colon for sense division.

Greek marks 'the Son of Man' with two articles (ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου); Latin renders it anarthrously as Filius hominis (Latin lacking the article), and the Syriac uses the construct/possessive ܒܪܗ ܕܐܢܫܐ ('the Son of Man'), each idiomatically appropriate to its language.
ἐκ νεκρῶν / ܡܢ ܡܝܬܐ / a mortuis

All three attest the resurrection verb (ἀναστῇ / ܩܡ / resurrexerit), but the Syriac ܡܐ ܕܩܡ places the verb immediately after the temporal conjunction at the head of the clause, preceding the subject 'Son of Man', whereas Greek and Latin keep the verb final after the subject.
